bills.notes: VERIFIED 2026-08-10 against the introduced text. Sponsor: Rep. AMATO - the paper never names the sponsor of the bill it identifies as the originator of Family C. Would create Mo. Rev. Stat. s 1.2045, self-titled the 'AI Non-Sentience and Responsibility Act'. Applies to AI systems developed, owned, deployed or operated on or after 28 August 2025. **ANSWERS THE LINEAGE QUESTION: OHIO COPIED MISSOURI, INCLUDING THE UNUSUAL PROVISIONS.** Both the alignment-washing clause (here at (12), Ohio s 1357.10) and the corporate-veil clause (here at (13), Ohio s 1357.11) ORIGINATE HERE. They are not Claggett's additions. Ohio's twelve sections map almost one-to-one onto this single section's fifteen subsections. **BUT OHIO INVERTED THE CORPORATE-VEIL PROVISION.** Missouri (13)(1): 'courts MAY PIERCE the corporate veil to hold parent companies... directly accountable if' the three triggers are met - a permissive grant to courts. Ohio s 1357.11(A): parent companies 'HAVE NO OBLIGATION TO, AND HAVE NO LIABILITY TO, any person... under the doctrine of piercing the corporate veil UNLESS' the same three triggers are demonstrated - default immunity with exceptions. Identical trigger language, opposite default. Missouri enables veil-piercing; Ohio grants immunity and carves out from it. **AND OHIO WEAKENED THE HUMAN-LIABILITY ANCHOR.** Missouri (10): an AI cannot bear fault 'as LIABILITY REMAINS WITH HUMAN ACTORS OR ENTITIES as described in this section.' Ohio s 1357.08 drops that clause entirely, leaving only that attempts to hold an AI liable are void. Wisconsin then drops affirmative human liability altogether. Across the family there is a clear gradient: Missouri anchors liability to humans most firmly, Ohio less so, Wisconsin not at all. That is the opposite of what the 'AI Non-Sentience and RESPONSIBILITY Act' name promises as the template travels, and it is directly relevant to Steinhauser's testimony that the bills exist to stop corporations shifting responsibility onto machines. **COPY-PASTE PROVEN TEXTUALLY:** 'Emergent properties' is defined at (2)(3) here and never used - and the identical unused definition reappears at Ohio s 1357.01(C). A defined-but-unused term surviving transplantation is about as clean a marker of copy-paste drafting as one could ask for, and it substantiates the paper's diffusion thesis at the level of text. The overbroad AI definition reaching 'rules-based logic' also originates here, not in Ohio. SOURCE NOTE: the house.mo.gov URL cited in the paper 404s; text supplied from the LegiScan record.

bills.provenance: Seeded from Smith, Caviola & Alexander (2026), Table 1, Figure 2 and 'Laws and Bills Cited'
bills.notes: VERIFIED 2026-08-10 against the As Introduced text. Would enact TWELVE new sections, Ohio Rev. Code ss 1357.01-1357.12. Sole sponsor as introduced: Rep. Claggett - no cosponsors on the introduced version. SUBSTANTIALLY WIDER THAN THE PAPER DESCRIBES. Beyond non-sentience (s 1357.02) it: voids marriage or union with an AI (s 1357.03); bars AI from serving as officer, director or manager (s 1357.04); bars property ownership including IP, financial accounts and digital assets (s 1357.05); assigns liability to owner/user with product-liability carve-outs for developers (s 1357.06); imposes oversight duties (s 1357.07); makes AI incapable of bearing liability (s 1357.08); requires safety mechanisms and risk assessments (s 1357.09); and imposes an incident-reporting duty for death, significant bodily harm or major property damage (s 1357.12). Six new provision tags were added to the schema to capture this. s 1357.10 IS REMARKABLE AND UNMENTIONED IN THE PAPER: labelling an AI system 'aligned', 'ethically trained' or 'value locked' does not on its own excuse or diminish liability. This is AI-safety vocabulary written into statutory text, and it anticipates alignment-washing. No other bill in the registry does anything comparable. s 1357.11 IS THE ONLY CORPORATE-VEIL PROVISION IN THE REGISTRY: it shields parent companies from veil-piercing EXCEPT where an AI subsidiary or shell was intentionally undercapitalised to evade damages, where corporate structure was used to obscure liability, or where the parent exercised direct control while shielding itself through layered entities. It therefore contemplates AI subsidiaries existing rather than barring them - hence affects_algorithmic_entity_formation='does_not_bar' - and it speaks directly to the A-Corp proposal in Arbel, Salib & Goldstein (2026). THE AI DEFINITION IS AS BROAD AS CRITICS CLAIMED: s 1357.01(A) reaches 'any software, machine, or system capable of simulating humanlike cognitive functions... based on data-driven algorithms, RULES-BASED LOGIC, or other computational methods'. 'Rules-based logic' is the textual basis for TechNet's and Cory Scott's objection that it captures spell checkers and navigation systems, and for the Alexander & Simon neural-implant argument. DRAFTING ARTIFACT: 'Emergent properties' is defined at s 1357.01(C) and then never used anywhere in the bill. CITATION NOTE: the header reads 136th General Assembly; the paper's reference-list entry for the Ohio committee page says '135th General Assembly'. The bill cite elsewhere in the paper says 136th, so the reference list is the error. STATUS NOT RE-CONFIRMED: this is the introduced text only; stage remains as the paper recorded it. LINEAGE VERIFIED 2026-08-10: derived from Missouri HB 1462, whose text has now been read. Ohio did not originate the alignment-washing or corporate-veil provisions - both are Missouri's. Ohio INVERTED the veil provision from permissive piercing into default parent-company immunity with the same three exceptions, and dropped Missouri's 'liability remains with human actors' clause from the AI-liability section.

bills.notes: VERIFIED 2026-08-10 against the House Committee Substitute text (HCS HBs 1746 & 1769, draft 3891H.04C) - the consolidated replacement the paper refers to. Would create Mo. Rev. Stat. s 1.2045, retitled the 'AI Nonsentience and Responsibility Act' (HB 1462 hyphenated 'Non-Sentience'). Effective 28 August 2026, with a grace period to 1 MARCH 2027 for anyone who formally adopted a compliance policy and demonstrated an implementation plan beforehand. **THE 2025-TO-2026 DIFF IS THE STORY. The personhood core is untouched; the responsibility half was substantially softened.** REMOVED: the entire corporate-veil-piercing provision, HB 1462 (13). The consolidated bill has no veil provision at all. That was the clause Steinhauser and the Alliance for Secure AI pointed to as closing the liability loophole, and Ohio kept a (inverted) version of it. Missouri simply deleted it. ADDED, a compliance safe harbour: (9) deems proper oversight demonstrated by adherence to Missouri AI risk-management standards 'derived from and based on the National Institute of Standards and Technology or NIST AI Risk Management Framework NIST AI 100-1', defaulting to the latest NIST version where Missouri is silent. This is the only bill in the registry that ties compliance to an external technical standard. ADDED, an absolution clause at (8): in cases of 'negligence, or gross negligence, or malpractice' the developer or deployer 'shall be absolved of any criminal wrongdoing or punitive damages' provided the subsection 9 standards were followed. ADDED, an open-source carve-out: 'Developer' now excludes anyone releasing an AI system 'free of charge using an Open Source Initiative approved license' - answering TechNet's objection that these bills burden open-source developers. DEFINITION REPLACED: 'AI' now takes 'the same meaning as used in 15 U.S.C. Section 9401(3)' - the federal National AI Initiative Act definition - in place of HB 1462's homegrown wording reaching 'rules-based logic'. The overbreadth criticism levelled at Ohio was answered in Missouri by adopting the federal statutory definition. ADDED (12)(2), technology neutrality: advances in software, automation, algorithmic decision-making or AI 'shall not be used as the basis for a deployer or developer to engage in conduct that is prohibited under the law'. TERMINOLOGY: 'Owner' became 'Deployer'; 'End-user' newly defined as someone who relies on but does not control the system. (10) still anchors liability to human actors, unlike Ohio and Wisconsin. DRAFTING ARTIFACT PERSISTS: 'Emergent properties' is redefined - now 'any unprogrammed or adaptive behavior of an AI system that appears to mimic human sentience' - and is still never used anywhere in the bill. APPARENT DRAFTING ERROR at (8): 'nor shall wrongdoing by the developer impute liability to the developer', which is circular and probably meant the user or deployer. Flagged, not corrected. SOURCE NOTE: the house.mo.gov URL cited in the paper 404s; text supplied from the LegiScan record. SCOPE OF THIS VERIFICATION: the consolidated HCS text has been read and verified; HB 1746's OWN introduced text has not. Its companion HB 1769 as introduced proved to be a verbatim HB 1462 clone, so HB 1746 as introduced probably was too, but that is an inference, not a reading.

bills.notes: VERIFIED 2026-08-10 against the introduced text. Introduced 29 Jan 2026, referred to the Assembly Committee on Science, Technology and AI. Nine Assembly authors and two Senate cosponsors (Jacque, Quinn); the paper names only Brill. The bill carries an '***AUTHORS SUBJECT TO CHANGE***' marker. HYBRID TECHNIQUE CONFIRMED ON THE FACE OF THE BILL: 'AN ACT to amend 990.01 (26); to create 134.44 of the statutes'. It both creates a standalone section and amends the general statutory definition of 'person'. The paper's claim that this is the only such bill holds. **IMPORTANT DIVERGENCE FROM OHIO AND MISSOURI.** Wisconsin does NOT assign liability to humans. s 134.44(2)(f) says only that AI 'is not a person against which liability may be imposed', and (2)(e) attributes ASSETS - not liability - to the developer, manufacturer or owner. There is no affirmative provision placing harm liability on any human, unlike Ohio s 1357.06. assigns_liability_to_humans has therefore been REMOVED and bars_ai_liability used instead. This is the textual basis for Daniel Barker's testimony that the bill creates an 'accountability vacuum' by denying AI personhood without assigning responsibility - the paper reports that objection; the text substantiates it. It also qualifies the paper's description of Family C as bills that 'clarify that human developers and users... are liable for any harms'. That is true of Ohio and Missouri, not of Wisconsin. THE AI DEFINITION IS THE OECD / EU AI ACT FORMULATION: 'an engineered or machine-based system that varies in its level of autonomy and that can, for explicit or implicit objectives, infer from the input it receives how to generate outputs that can influence physical or virtual environments.' This is materially narrower and more standard than Ohio's, which reaches 'rules-based logic'. Definitional quality varies enormously across the registry and is worth surfacing as a comparison axis. 'Owner' expressly EXCLUDES the end user, again unlike Ohio. VOIDING IS ASYMMETRIC: sub. (3) voids actions contrary to (2)(c) - marriage - only. Appointments to corporate office and property transfers are prohibited but not declared void, where Ohio voids both. CORPORATE PERSONHOOD EXPRESSLY RETAINED in the amended s 990.01(26): 'Person' still 'includes all partnerships, associations and bodies politic or corporate'. STATUS NOT CONFIRMED: this is the introduced text. The paper records the bill as Failed; after Washington HB 2029 turned out to be wrongly recorded as failed, the final disposition still needs checking.

bills.notes: VERIFIED 2026-08-10 against Public Chapter No. 781 (TN Secretary of State). Enacted as SB 837, with HB 849 substituted out on 8 April 2026. Amends Tenn. Code Ann. s 1-3-105(a) by deleting subdivision (20) and substituting a new definition of 'person'. Effective on becoming law (23 April 2026); Public Chapter filed 28 April 2026. SCOPE DIFFERS FROM THE PAPER IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: the enacted text reaches only 'person' - the original draft's 'life' and 'natural person' terms were dropped along with the fetal-personhood provisions - but the exclusion itself is much wider than AI, covering 'a computer algorithm, a software program, computer hardware, or any type of machine'. 'Any type of machine' is the broadest exclusionary language in the whole registry. The same subdivision expressly RETAINS corporate personhood at (A), so the corporate carve-out is an express inclusion inside the amended definition rather than a separate saving clause. SPONSORS NOT IN THE PAPER: Senate - Pody, Gardenhire, Bowling; House - Reneau, Bulso, Helton-Haynes, Reedy, Pearson, Todd, Powers. Rep. Justin Pearson is a Democrat, so this enacted exclusion bill had cross-party sponsorship (6R-1D), which qualifies the paper's 'primarily Republican-sponsored' framing. A SECOND AMENDMENT, HA0979, is recorded alongside SA0922; the paper mentions only SA0922. Committee votes were unanimous: House Judiciary 17-0, Civil Justice Subcommittee 6-0.

bills.provenance: Seeded from Smith, Caviola & Alexander (2026), Table 1, Figure 2 and 'Laws and Bills Cited'
bills.notes: VERIFIED 2026-08-10 against Public Chapter No. 1066 (TN Secretary of State). Enacted as SB 1493, with HB 1455 substituted out. Passed 23 April 2026, effective on becoming law. CONFIRMS THE PAPER: the enacted text does NOT felonise AI training and does NOT address AI legal status or consciousness. It directs TACIR to study AI risk and report to the governor and both speakers by 31 JANUARY 2027 - a dated future event the tracker should watch. BUT THE SUBJECT MATTER SURVIVED AS RESEARCH QUESTIONS: study item (b)(5) covers 'the risks of an artificial intelligence chatbot engaging with a user as if the chatbot is a human and providing emotional support, mental health care, or health care', and item (b)(4) covers regulating or prohibiting dangerous prompts such as encouragement to commit suicide. Those map almost item-for-item onto the prohibitions in the introduced bill. The amendment converted felonies into a research agenda rather than abandoning the topic - a distinct legislative move worth naming, and a plausible route back to substantive regulation in 2027. UNCODIFIED: the caption says it amends Tit. 29, 33, 39 and 47, but the enacted text amends no code section at all - it is a freestanding study directive. The caption is residue from the far broader bill as introduced. SPONSORS: Senate - Massey, Yager. House - thirteen members, including Rep. Justin Pearson and Rep. Karen Camper, both Democrats. As with Pub. Ch. 781, sponsorship was cross-party.
